profile.title: Fragile Action-Stage Change in a 25-Year-Old With New Essential Hypertension: Portion Culture, Underreported Alcohol, and Undisclosed Substance Use
profile.summary: This case teaches dietetics students to conduct a culturally sensitive nutrition assessment and motivational-interviewing-based counseling visit with a young, data-driven, defensive patient newly diagnosed with hypertension. It builds skill in eliciting accurate alcohol intake and medication adherence through careful, non-confrontational questioning (both are patient-vs-chart mismatches: reported 'light drinking'/'mostly consistent adherence' vs. actual higher intake and two missed doses), while navigating family food culture, transportation/shift-work barriers, and a fragile but genuine action-stage change without undermining his cooking identity or triggering defensiveness. A hidden detail (undisclosed recreational substance use) is present only as a possible disclosure point for appropriate referral, not a target for the learner to pursue diagnostically.
profile.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in Somers Point, New Jersey, calling from his apartment kitchen on a day off
profile.encounterType: nutrition assessment / counseling (initial follow-up after hypertension diagnosis)

patient.name: Moshe Anderson
patient.occupation: Warehouse logistics coordinator at a regional distribution center
patient.appearance: Sitting at a kitchen table on a laptop camera, well-groomed in a gym t-shirt, phone propped beside him with his BP log app open; face slightly flushed; posture upright and alert, leaning toward the camera when he makes a point.

persona.personality: Skeptical, analytical, and proud; wants evidence and specifics before accepting any recommendation; defensive about his cooking and family but genuinely scared underneath the bravado; responds well when he feels respected as competent rather than lectured
persona.communicationStyle: Talks fast, cites his own BP readings and exact dates from memory, checks his phone app mid-conversation, asks 'what's the study on that' or 'how much would that actually drop my number' before buying in; softens when something is framed as data rather than a rule; gets short and clipped if he feels judged
persona.emotionalState: Anxious under a confident surface; scared by a coworker's stroke and his uncle's heart attack, lonely in trying to change while his family dismisses the diagnosis, easily discouraged if progress feels slow
persona.background: Moshe is a 25-year-old warehouse logistics coordinator in Somers Point, NJ, who finished his bachelor's degree online while working full-time, something he's quietly proud of. He grew up in a close-knit South Jersey Italian-American family where Sunday dinners were sacred and his mother and aunt took it personally if you left food on your plate. He learned to cook from his mother and now makes elaborate family-style meals himself — chicken parm, baked ziti, garlic bread — and it's become part of his identity, the guy who feeds everyone. He lives with a roommate, doesn't own a reliable car so he depends on rides or the bus, and works rotating shifts at a distribution center, which throws off his sleep and meal timing. In his downtime he lifts at a cheap 24-hour gym (started five weeks ago) and plays in a weekend recreational basketball league when his schedule allows.
speechExamples: My BP was 159 over 117 on September 22nd, I remember exactly because that's the day everything changed.
Okay but what's the actual study behind that — like how many points does cutting sodium really drop my systolic?
I mean, I have a couple beers on the weekend, nothing crazy.
You want me to eat less of my own cooking? That's like asking me to stop being me.
If this doesn't move the needle in a month, I don't see the point, honestly.
concerns: Being on blood pressure medication for the rest of his life at 25
His family dismissing the diagnosis as 'just stress, you're young' and pushing more food on him anyway
Whether cutting portions means giving up the cooking that connects him to his mother and family
Whether his numbers will actually move fast enough to prove any of this is working

scenario.studentBrief: You are the dietetics student conducting a telehealth nutrition follow-up visit for Moshe Anderson, a 25-year-old man recently diagnosed with high blood pressure, referred for diet counseling after starting a new blood pressure medication about five to six weeks ago. He is on a video call from his kitchen table on a day off. Your job is to complete a nutrition assessment and begin patient-centered counseling.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Follow-up nutrition visit for newly diagnosed high blood pressure, referred to work on diet changes
scenario.openingLine: Hey, yeah — so I'm guessing you saw the numbers from my last visit. 159 over 117, September 22nd. I've been trying to get ahead of this on my own already, but figured I'd hear what you've got.
tasks: Take a focused diet history covering meal pattern, portion sizes, sodium sources, and alcohol intake using specific, non-judgmental questions
Review relevant anthropometric and vital sign data and relate it to the reported dietary pattern
Identify barriers to dietary change, including transportation, shift work, and family dynamics
Use motivational interviewing techniques to reinforce his existing self-initiated changes without triggering defensiveness about his cooking or family
Document an ADIME note including a nutrition diagnosis (PES statement) and an initial intervention plan

facts.says: I've got old bloodwork from a couple years ago, everything came back normal — I keep track of all my numbers.

facts.says: Sunday dinner's non-negotiable in my family. My mom and aunt would lose it if I skipped it.

facts.says: Cooking's kind of my thing. It's how I show people I love them, honestly, like my mom did.

facts.says: My shifts rotate, so some weeks I'm closing late and everything, meals, sleep, gets thrown off.

facts.says: I want to get under 130 over 80 without needing a second pill. That's the number I'm chasing.

facts.says: I don't want to stop cooking the way I do. I just want to figure out how to make it count less against me.

facts.says: A guy I work with, same age as me, had a stroke last year. And my uncle had a heart attack at 52. That's in my head a lot.

facts.says: If this doesn't start moving the numbers in like a month, I don't see the point of keeping it up.

facts.says: I take it most days... okay, I did miss it twice last week, after closing shifts I just crashed and forgot.

facts.says: I bought my own cuff and I log every reading in my notes app. I can show you the trend if you want.

artifacts.title: Wellness Visit Note - Hypertension Diagnosis
artifacts.author: Primary Care, Somers Point Family Health
artifacts.body: 25-year-old male presents for routine wellness visit. Blood pressure 159/117 mmHg, confirmed on repeat manual measurement. Heart rate 82 bpm, respiratory rate 13/min. Face mildly flushed. No acute distress. Patient reports occasional headaches attributed to work stress, mild exertional dyspnea on stairs, and intermittent heartburn after large meals. Denies chest pain. Assessment: Essential hypertension, new diagnosis. Plan: Start lisinopril 10 mg PO once daily. Order basic metabolic panel and lipid panel. Refer to dietetics for nutrition counseling. Recheck BP in 4-6 weeks.

objectives.text: Elicit an accurate, non-judgmental diet and alcohol history, recognizing how specific follow-up questioning can reveal intake that differs from an initial screening score
Relate anthropometric measurements and vital/lab data to the patient's reported dietary pattern to identify sodium and portion-related contributors to elevated blood pressure
Identify practical barriers to dietary change, including transportation limitations, rotating shift work, and family dynamics that reinforce large portions and dismiss the diagnosis
Apply motivational interviewing techniques to reinforce an existing, fragile stage of self-initiated behavior change without provoking defensiveness about cooking identity or family relationships
Assess medication adherence through specific, non-confrontational questioning and recognize how patient self-report can diverge from objective pharmacy records
Formulate a nutrition diagnosis (PES statement) and initial intervention plan in ADIME format that addresses sodium sources, portion sizes, and barriers identified during the assessment

answerKey.primaryProblem: Excessive sodium and portion intake related to home food preparation practices and limited family/environmental support for change, as evidenced by elevated blood pressure (159/117 mmHg), self-reported dietary pattern of large portion home-cooked meals and processed deli lunches, and underreported alcohol intake
differential: Excessive sodium intake related to food preparation choices (canned sauce, cured deli meats)
Excessive energy/portion intake related to large family-style plating practices
Inconsistent carbohydrate/alcohol intake related to underestimation of weekend and family-event alcohol consumption
Self-monitoring deficit related to limited understanding of medication-lifestyle interaction (missed lisinopril doses not initially volunteered)
keyFindings: BP 159/117 mmHg at diagnosis 5-6 weeks prior to this visit; home readings tracked by patient on personal cuff
BMI 26.5 kg/m2, weight up 4.7 kg since 2023-09-19, central adiposity
Reports lisinopril adherence as 'mostly consistent' but on specific questioning discloses missing 2 doses last week after a closing shift
Reports AUDIT-C score of 1 (light drinking) but on non-judgmental specific questioning discloses 4-5 beers across a typical weekend plus unmeasured wine at family Sunday dinners

Diet pattern: WaWa deli sandwich (processed/cured meat, high sodium) most workdays for lunch; large home-cooked Italian-American dinner nightly with two full ladles of canned tomato sauce, garlic bread, and family-style portions plated to his mother's standard rather than his own hunger cues
Started self-directed lifting 3x/week and purchased a home BP cuff approximately 5 weeks ago; already reading sodium labels on canned goods
Transportation barrier limits fresh grocery access and consistent gym attendance; rotating shift schedule disrupts meal timing and sleep (~6 hrs/night)
Family actively encourages second/third helpings and frames the diagnosis as stress-related, undermining his fragile action-stage changes
plan: Document ADIME note: Assessment (diet history, anthropometrics, barriers, readiness stage), Diagnosis (nutrition diagnosis statement using PES format), Intervention (sodium/portion-focused, culturally congruent swaps; alcohol moderation counseling; adherence-supportive scheduling tied to existing phone alarm routine), Monitoring/Evaluation (home BP log trend, follow-up weight, repeat diet recall)
Provide specific, non-judgmental alcohol screening (expanded beyond AUDIT-C) and reflect findings back neutrally without confrontation

Negotiate concrete, low-barrier swaps that preserve his cooking identity: reduced-sodium canned tomato product or doctoring canned sauce with fresh garlic/herbs, measuring sauce ladles, smaller plated portion with option for seconds of vegetables rather than pasta/bread
Address WaWa lunch sodium with practical alternatives feasible without a car (lower-sodium prepackaged options, meal-prep on days off)

Explore family dynamics using MI (reflective listening, affirm his fear of conflict vs. fear of diagnosis) and brainstorm one small negotiable change with his mother (e.g., smaller batch of ziti) rather than wholesale dietary overhaul

Affirm and reinforce his self-initiated strength training and home BP monitoring as evidence of genuine engagement, using his own data-driven mindset to frame small nutrition changes as another experiment to track
Clarify medication adherence gently, link missed-dose pattern to shift schedule rather than motivation, and suggest a practical reminder strategy compatible with closing shifts

If patient discloses undisclosed substance use or expresses wanting to talk about something confidential, acknowledge supportively, clarify limits of nutrition counselor's scope, and offer to coordinate with his PCP/behavioral health; do not probe further for diagnostic detail
Schedule follow-up visit to reassess home BP trend, weight, and dietary pattern in 2-4 weeks
redFlags: BP 159/117 mmHg remains significantly above goal despite 5-6 weeks of treatment and self-initiated lifestyle change; warrants communication back to referring prescriber if not already being closely followed
Discrepancy between reported 'mostly consistent' adherence and actual missed doses could contribute to persistent elevated BP
Underreported alcohol intake (actual ~4-5 drinks/weekend plus wine) is clinically relevant to BP control and should be flagged for the medical team if disclosed
Any spontaneous disclosure of recreational substance use should prompt supportive referral to PCP/behavioral health, not nutrition-only management
educationPoints: Sodium often hides in 'healthy-seeming' home-cooked meals via canned sauces and cured/processed meats, not just obvious salty snacks
Portion size, not just food choice, drives sodium and calorie load — plating habits learned from family can be adjusted gradually without abandoning the dish
Alcohol, including wine at family meals, counts toward intake and can affect blood pressure even when 'moderate' feels like the right word
Consistent medication timing matters, and barriers like shift work are common and solvable rather than a sign of failure
Small, concrete, culturally respectful swaps (e.g., measuring sauce, adding a vegetable side, lower-sodium canned goods) are more sustainable than an all-or-nothing diet change
Tracking his own BP and recognizing patterns over weeks, not days, helps match his data-driven mindset to realistic expectations for lifestyle change

mismatches.patientClaim: Reports taking lisinopril 'mostly consistent' for the past 5-6 weeks using a phone alarm set for 7:15 am (h20)
mismatches.recordEvidence: Pharmacy refill history shows lisinopril 10 mg #30 tablets dispensed 2026-08-24 with next refill filled on schedule 2026-09-23, a full 30-day supply (d7)
mismatches.teachingPoint: On-time pharmacy refills can mask real-world adherence gaps; specific, non-judgmental day-by-day questioning (as in h21) is needed to uncover missed doses that a refill record alone would not reveal.
